body_html:
Sentence mining is the habit of collecting real sentences from what you read and hear, instead of memorizing single words. Rather than writing “ganas = desire” on a card, you save Tengo muchas ganas de verte (“I really want to see you”). The sentence carries grammar, rhythm and feeling with it, so you remember it better and can actually use it. Here is how sentence mining works in Spanish and a simple routine to start today.

Key takeaways
  • Save whole sentences, not lonely words.
  • Choose sentences that are almost fully understandable, with one new thing in them.
  • Review a little every day, ideally with spaced repetition.
  • Prefer sentences you would genuinely say or love to read again.
{{toc}}

Why sentence mining works

Words don’t live alone. In Spanish, a single verb changes with every person and tense, nouns carry gender, and many expressions can’t be translated word by word. A sentence keeps all that information together. When you review Me olvidé de llamarte (“I forgot to call you”), you are also learning that olvidarse takes de, how the past tense sounds and where the pronoun goes.

Sentence mining also fits naturally with {{link:comprehensible-input-spanish|comprehensible input}}. You collect from material you already understand, so each sentence comes with meaning and context attached.

How to choose good sentences

  • One new thing. The ideal sentence is fully understandable except for one new word or structure. Language learners sometimes call this an “i+1 sentence”.
  • Short and complete. Five to fifteen words is perfect.
  • Useful or beautiful. Choose lines you would say in real life, or ones that move you.
  • From real sources. Books, songs, series, conversations. Natural Spanish beats invented examples.
{{image:2}}

Where to mine Spanish sentences

Almost anything you enjoy can be a source:

  • Bilingual books. The English is right there, so you know exactly what each sentence means. See {{link:bilingual-books-english-spanish|how to use English–Spanish bilingual books}}.
  • Parallel texts. Comparing lines side by side shows you how ideas change between languages; I explain the method in {{link:parallel-text-reading|parallel text reading}}.
  • Songs and series. Lyrics and dialogue are full of everyday expressions.
  • Your own life. When you wish you knew how to say something, look it up and save the sentence.
{{book:love-slowly}}

A simple sentence mining routine

  1. Read or listen for ten minutes as usual.
  2. Pick one or two sentences that are nearly clear but contain something new.
  3. Write them down with the English meaning and, optionally, a short note: echar de menos = to miss (Spain).
  4. Say them aloud two or three times.
  5. Review your collection for five minutes the next day, then a few days later, then a week later.

Paper notebook or flashcard app?

NotebookFlashcard app
Best forSlow, reflective learners who like handwritingLearners who want automatic review timing
StrengthWriting by hand helps memorySpaced repetition shows cards just before you forget
Watch out forForgetting to reviewAdding too many cards and burning out

A popular free option is Anki, which uses spaced repetition. Put the Spanish sentence on the front and the meaning on the back, or hide the new word and try to recall it in context.

{{image:3}}

Examples of good sentences to mine

SentenceMeaningWhat it teaches
Me cuesta levantarme temprano.It’s hard for me to get up early.costar used like gustar
Acabo de llegar.I’ve just arrived.acabar de + infinitive
Se me olvidó la llave.I forgot the key.Accidental se
Ojalá que puedas venir.I hope you can come.Subjunctive after ojalá
Echo de menos a mi familia.I miss my family.Spain’s phrase for “to miss”

Notice that each sentence teaches one useful structure you can reuse with your own words. That is the real power of sentence mining: you are not collecting trivia, you are collecting templates.

Turn mined sentences into your own Spanish

Once a sentence feels familiar, change one part of it. Me cuesta levantarme temprano becomes Me cuesta hablar en público (“It’s hard for me to speak in public”). Acabo de llegar becomes Acabo de comer. This tiny step moves the sentence from recognition to production, and it is the bridge between reading and speaking. Saying your new versions aloud, or writing them in a short journal entry, makes the pattern yours.

How long until you notice results?

Most learners notice the first effect within two or three weeks: sentences they mined start appearing in their reading, and they recognize them instantly. After a couple of months, mined patterns begin to pop out in their own speech, often without planning. Keep the habit small and steady, and trust that each saved sentence is quietly doing its work.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Mining too much. Two good sentences a day beats twenty you will never review.
  • Choosing sentences that are too hard. If you need three dictionary lookups, it is not the right sentence yet.
  • Skipping review. Collecting is fun; reviewing is what makes it stick.
  • Never saying them aloud. Your mouth needs practice too.

Sentence mining is one of many small habits that make Spanish part of your daily life. My complete guide to {{link:bilingual-english-and-spanish|bilingual English and Spanish}} shows how it fits with reading, listening and speaking.

Final thoughts

Sentence mining turns everything you read into a personal phrasebook. Choose sentences that are almost clear, save a couple each day, say them aloud and review them gently. Over months, that small collection becomes the Spanish you naturally reach for.

faq.a: Sentence mining is collecting real sentences from Spanish you read or hear and reviewing them, instead of memorizing isolated words.

faq.q: How many sentences should I mine per day?
faq.a: One to five is plenty for most learners. Quality and regular review matter more than quantity.

faq.q: Do I need Anki for sentence mining?
faq.a: No. A paper notebook works well if you review it regularly. Apps like Anki simply automate the timing of reviews.
